title: Detraining and plateaus

draft.title: Detraining and plateaus
card: the loss of fitness gains when training is reduced or stops. It can happen after injury, illness or a long break.
a stage where progress stalls even though training carries on. The body has adapted to the same program and no longer gets a new challenge.
A plateau can be broken by changing the program. For example, the intensity, time or type of training can be changed.
Detraining is fixed by starting to train again. A plateau is different: the athlete is still training, but the program needs to change.
draft.remember: Detraining is fitness lost when training stops. A plateau is progress stalling while training goes on.

a.q: Which situation is an example of a plateau?
opts: A runner trains the same way for months and stops improving
A runner breaks a leg and loses fitness during recovery
A runner stops training for the summer and slows down
A runner takes a week off and feels less fit on return
a.why: A plateau is when progress stalls while training continues. The other three involve training stopping, which is detraining. The first runner is still training, so the stall is a plateau.
a.clue: In which case is the athlete still training?

b.q: Tom, a rower in Ballarat, has done the same weekly program for four months. His 2000 m time has not changed for six weeks. What is the best response?
opts: Change the intensity or type of training in his program
Stop training for a few weeks so he can recover fully
Repeat the same program, as it has worked before
Treat it as detraining and start training again
b.why: Tom is still training, so this is a plateau, not detraining. His body has adapted to the same program, so it needs a change such as new intensity or type. Resting fully risks detraining, which would cost him fitness.
b.clue: Is Tom still training, or has he stopped?

a.best: A runner trains the same way for months and stops improving

b.best: Change the intensity or type of training in his program

problems.detail: Why (a) says 'The first runner is still training', but options are shown in random order and the plateau option is not necessarily first (here it is second). Refer to the runner who trains the same way for months instead.

The remember line says detraining is fitness lost 'when training stops', but the card defines it as loss when training is 'reduced or stops'. Students could come away thinking reduced training cannot cause detraining.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer and the facts are sound. Why (a) refers to 'the first runner', which breaks under random option order, and the remember line drops 'reduced' from the detraining definition.
